opus-5.5.text:
Llama 2 is a really useful model for this kind of research, mainly because it's open. With multiagent debate, where several instances of a language model propose answers, read each other's responses, critique them, and revise over a few rounds, much of the interesting science is in understanding *why* the process helps. Open weights let you look inside. You can study the model's internal representations as it updates its beliefs, fine-tune it on the outputs of debate, and run many experiments without hitting an API budget or having the underlying model change from week to week.

When we first did the debate work, we mostly used closed models like ChatGPT, and the main limitation was that we could only treat them as black boxes. With Llama 2 you can close the loop. You can run debate to get more accurate, more consistent answers, then use those answers as feedback to train the model itself. That's very much in the spirit of AI feedback: the model's own collective reasoning becomes a supervision signal.

There is a caveat. Debate works best when the individual agents are reasonably capable. If a model can't recognize a good argument when it sees one, the agents can just reinforce each other's mistakes and converge on a confident wrong answer. With the smaller Llama 2 models, you do see weaker gains on harder reasoning tasks than with the stronger proprietary models. The 70B model is much better at it. So I'd say Llama 2 is a great research platform. It's maybe not the ceiling of what debate can do, but it's an excellent place to understand the mechanisms and to build methods that will scale as open models get stronger.

r002.rationale: It says smaller Llama 2 models show weaker gains on harder tasks and that less capable agents can reinforce mistakes, but it does not state that models substantially weaker than GPT-3.5 make improvements through debate or AI feedback difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think Llama 2 was actually a really interesting model for that line of work, mostly because of what it enabled from a research standpoint rather than because it was the strongest model at the time.

When we were doing the multiagent debate work, one of the big questions was whether these improvements come from the specific model or whether they're a more general property of having multiple language models critique and revise each other's answers. With a closed model, you can run the experiments, but you're limited to what the API gives you. You can't look at the weights, you can't fine-tune in a controlled way, and the model can change underneath you between runs. Having an open model like Llama 2 meant that we could actually hold the model fixed, run many rounds of debate, and look carefully at where the agreement among agents comes from and whether it correlates with correctness.

Now, in terms of capability, Llama 2 was clearly weaker than GPT-4 at reasoning. And that mattered, because debate and AI feedback methods depend on the model being able to recognize that another agent's answer is wrong, or that its own reasoning has a mistake. If the base model can't identify errors, then multiple copies of it talking to each other tend to just converge on a shared wrong answer. We did see that failure mode more with smaller open models. So one takeaway was that these methods amplify whatever critical ability is already there. They don't create it out of nothing.

The other thing I'd say is that the Llama 2 chat models were trained with pretty heavy preference tuning, and that showed up in debate. The models were sometimes overly agreeable. They'd defer to another agent's answer even when their own was better, which is sort of the opposite of what you want in a debate setting. We had to think carefully about prompting to get them to actually push back rather than just being polite.

So overall, I'd say it was a very useful model for understanding the mechanisms behind these methods, and for making the research reproducible. But if the goal was to get the best absolute performance out of debate or AI feedback, you still wanted a stronger base model. I think that gap has narrowed a lot since then with the newer open models, which is exciting, because it means a lot more people can do this kind of research.

astra-6.text:
I think Llama 2 is an exciting platform for that research because having access to the model lets you study more than just its final answers. You can fine-tune it, set up different ways for models to debate each other, and investigate whether feedback actually improves the result.

The distinction I’d make is between producing a convincing argument and producing a correct one. If two models agree after a debate, that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ve found the truth—they may share the same blind spots. So I’d treat Llama 2 as a useful experimental platform, but evaluate debate and AI feedback against tasks where we can independently check whether the answers improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Llama 2 is a useful platform for that research, particularly because having access to the model weights gives you more control over the experiments. You can study how models critique one another, whether debate actually improves an answer, and how you might use that feedback for training.

The main caveat is that agreement isn’t necessarily evidence of correctness. Two models can share the same misconception, or one can produce a persuasive argument that’s wrong. So I’d assess it by whether the interaction improves performance on tasks where we can independently verify the answer, rather than just whether the debate sounds convincing.
